content: A febrile seizure, also referred to as a fever fit or febrile convulsion, is a type of generalized seizure that occurs in response to an elevated body temperature. These seizures are most commonly observed in children under the age of three. They are not typically diagnosed in children younger than six months or older than six years. In many cases, the seizure itself may be the first indication of a fever. It is hypothesized that the rapid rise in body temperature, rather than the absolute temperature reached, is the primary trigger for these seizures. Febrile seizures can be classified into two main categories: simple and complex. A simple febrile seizure is characterized by a duration of less than 15 minutes, generalized seizure activity, and no recurrence during the same febrile illness. In contrast, a complex febrile seizure may involve focal features, last longer than 15 minutes, or recur within 24 hours. The occurrence of febrile seizures is thought to result from the interplay between a genetically and age-determined low seizure threshold and an external trigger, such as fever. Some children are more predisposed to seizures under specific conditions due to this low threshold. While the genetic basis of febrile seizures is still under investigation, certain mutations that increase neuronal excitability have been identified as potential contributors. The diagnosis of a febrile seizure is made by excluding more serious causes of seizures, such as meningitis or encephalitis. It is essential to seek medical evaluation, and in many cases, the child may be admitted to the hospital for observation and diagnostic testing. If the child returns to a normal state of health shortly after the seizure, it is less likely that a central nervous system infection is present. Even when a febrile seizure is diagnosed, physicians will aim to identify and treat the underlying cause of the fever. A simple febrile seizure is defined by its short duration (less than 15 minutes), generalized nature, and lack of recurrence within 24 hours. This type of seizure is the most common and is generally less concerning. In contrast, a complex febrile seizure is longer in duration, may recur within 24 hours, or may involve focal features. Simple febrile seizures are reassuring in that they typically do not cause permanent brain damage, are unlikely to recur frequently as the child ages, and do not significantly increase the risk of developing epilepsy in adulthood (less than 3-5%, which is comparable to the general population). Certain factors may indicate a higher likelihood of future afebrile seizures or epilepsy in children with febrile seizures. These include a family history of afebrile seizures in first-degree relatives, pre-existing neurological abnormalities or developmental delays, febrile seizures lasting longer than 15 minutes, and febrile seizures with focal features. Management of febrile seizures often involves addressing the fever itself. The early use of antipyretic medications, such as acetaminophen or ibuprofen, is considered effective. However, physical cooling methods, such as tepid sponging, are no longer recommended as they do not provide additional benefits over antipyretics. There is limited evidence to support the use of antipyretics to prevent febrile seizures following childhood vaccinations. While some children experience frequent febrile seizures, the routine use of anti-epileptic medications is generally not recommended due to the unfavorable risk-to-benefit ratio. The prognosis for febrile seizures is generally favorable. Following a first febrile seizure, approximately 2-4% of children may experience an unprovoked (afebrile) seizure, which is about four times the risk in the general population. Most of these children will go on to develop epilepsy. Risk factors for developing epilepsy include a family history of epilepsy, complex febrile seizures, and early-onset neurodevelopmental abnormalities. While prolonged febrile seizures have been associated with temporal lobe lesions, such as hippocampal sclerosis, it is now believed that these brain abnormalities likely predate the febrile seizure and increase the likelihood of its occurrence. Recurrence of febrile seizures is relatively common, with approximately one-third of children experiencing another episode. The strongest predictor of recurrence is the age at which the first febrile seizure occurs; younger children are more likely to have recurrent episodes before they outgrow the condition. Most recurrences occur within the first year after the initial seizure, and over 90% occur within two years. Additional risk factors for recurrence include a family history of febrile seizures, an initial seizure occurring at a relatively low fever, and multiple seizures during the same febrile illness. Interestingly, status epilepticus in an otherwise healthy child does not appear to significantly increase the risk of further febrile seizures or the development of epilepsy.
